rationale: Both are recurring biodiversity observation releases. Their regeneration rules differ, making release snapshots essential for reconstructing what was knowable at a given date.
Both support long-term paleobiological reconstruction; specimen identifiers and stratigraphic context can provide future crosswalk opportunities without assuming the same specimens are represented.
Fossil fish otoliths can be compared with museum paleobiology records as an independent collection layer; any taxonomic match requires specimen-level verification.
Both preserve herbarium material and historical determinations, enabling future taxonomic synonym and geographic-history reconciliation.
Both illustrate digitization of historically accumulated cryptogam collections; absence from a public release should not be interpreted as absence from the physical collection.
Both are Smithsonian NMNH collection datasets and should retain stable institutional provenance while keeping fossil and extant collection domains distinct.
Both demonstrate why collection identifiers, former subcollections, and type-specimen provenance must survive migrations and consolidation.
Both represent digitization states of large physical collections; longitudinal release comparison can expose newly surfaced specimens and corrected determinations.
Both depend on community observations and quality rules, but their licensing, consent, spatial generalization, and regeneration semantics differ and must remain distinct.
Both provide institution-level collection metadata useful for reconstructing historical specimen custody and future paleobiological reanalysis.
Large herbarium datasets can support independent distribution-history comparisons, but geography and collection effort must be modeled before ecological inference.
Both require preservation of historical determinations alongside modern taxonomic mappings to avoid destroying the evidentiary trail.
